facts.title: Ninety-two queens
facts.detail: Eight queens can occupy an otherwise empty board without attacking one another in 92 arrangements. Treating rotations and reflections as the same leaves just 12.

facts.title: A knight can visit every square
facts.detail: A knight’s tour visits all 64 squares exactly once. In a closed tour, its final square is one knight move from its starting square.

facts.title: Why odd boards break closed knight tours
facts.detail: Every knight move switches square color. That simple fact proves that a closed knight tour on a board with an odd number of squares is impossible.

facts.title: Two corners break the domino puzzle
facts.detail: Remove two opposite corners from a chessboard and 31 dominoes can no longer cover it. Both corners share a color; every domino must cover one square of each color.

facts.title: A rook can hold a queen to a draw
facts.detail: In a fortress, the stronger side may have no way to make progress. Some carefully arranged rook-and-pawn fortresses hold against a queen despite the material deficit.

facts.title: A square can be mined
facts.detail: In a trebuchet position, two kings defend mutually attacked pawns. Whoever must move first loses a pawn: the turn itself becomes a disadvantage.

facts.title: A king can chase two targets at once
facts.detail: Réti’s 1921 study draws because a king approaches an enemy pawn and supports its own pawn along the same diagonal. Moving diagonally need not cost extra moves.

facts.title: A rook promotion can save the win
facts.detail: The Saavedra study requires promotion to a rook. Choosing a queen allows a stalemate trick; the less powerful piece keeps a winning threat alive.

facts.title: The board has 204 squares
facts.detail: There are 64 one-by-one squares, but also 49 two-by-two squares, 36 three-by-three squares, and so on. Add all eight sizes to get 204.

facts.title: A five-queen covering puzzle
facts.detail: Five queens suffice to attack or occupy every square on an otherwise empty 8×8 board. Four cannot do it. This is a domination problem, distinct from the eight-queens puzzle.

facts.title: The first move can arrive last
facts.detail: A move-order transposition reaches the same position through different moves. Opening names describe a route; the resulting position, side to move and available rights determine what can happen next.

facts.title: A sacrifice can be temporary
facts.detail: In a desperado combination, an already doomed piece captures something before disappearing. Its apparent sacrifice may recover material that would otherwise be lost.

facts.title: A piece can block its own army
facts.detail: An interference sacrifice places a piece on a line between two enemy pieces. Capturing it may obstruct a different defender, which is the point of a Novotny theme.

facts.title: A move can threaten nothing
facts.detail: A waiting move in a composed problem can create zugzwang: it makes no direct threat, yet every legal reply gives something away.

facts.title: A bishop can be trapped by its own strength
facts.detail: A bishop controls only one square color, so the wrong rook-pawn corner can be a draw even with an extra bishop and pawn. The defending king must actually reach the safe corner.

facts.title: The longest-known forced mates exceed the move limit
facts.detail: Seven-piece tablebases contain positions requiring more than 500 moves to mate with perfect resistance when the fifty-move rule is ignored. A theoretical win is not always a tournament win.

facts.title: A computer champion ran on a phone
facts.detail: Pocket Fritz 4 won the 2009 Copa Mercosur with 9½/10 while running on an HTC Touch HD. Its search speed was tiny beside desktop engines, showing the value of evaluation and software.

facts.title: A chess program played by hand
facts.detail: Turing’s Turochamp algorithm was conceived before a suitable computer was available to him. He manually simulated it in a 1952 game against Alick Glennie.

facts.title: Chess moves by electric telegraph
facts.detail: The 1844 correspondence match between Washington and Baltimore used the new electric telegraph. Moves traveled faster than mailed letters long before internet chess.

facts.title: An international match by radio
facts.detail: The 1945 USA–USSR radio match connected players in New York and Moscow. The Soviet team won 15½–4½ without the teams sharing a room.

facts.title: A Candidates tournament on an island
facts.detail: The 1962 Candidates tournament took place in Curaçao, with eight players meeting four times each. Tigran Petrosian won without losing a game.

facts.title: A champion was also a mathematician
facts.detail: Max Euwe earned a doctorate in mathematics in 1926, became world chess champion in 1935, and later served as FIDE president.

facts.title: A world champion wrote about philosophy
facts.detail: Emanuel Lasker earned a mathematics doctorate and wrote philosophical works, including Kampf. His chess title reign lasted from 1894 to 1921.

facts.title: One sister broke Fischer’s age record
facts.detail: Judit Polgár became a grandmaster in 1991 at 15 years and 4 months, younger than Fischer had been. She later reached eighth in the world on a FIDE rating list.

facts.title: Chess once had adjournment strategy
facts.detail: Before powerful portable engines, long games could be paused with a sealed move. Players and their teams analyzed overnight, making preparation part of the unfinished game.

facts.title: A sealed move could lose without being played
facts.detail: Under adjournment rules, an ambiguous or illegal sealed move could cost the game when the envelope was opened. Players had to record the exact move, not just an intention.

facts.title: Fischer’s random chess still has rules
facts.detail: Chess960 has 960 legal starting arrangements: bishops must stand on opposite colors, and the king must be between the rooks. Not every shuffle qualifies.

facts.title: The mirror of a game can change who wins
facts.detail: In the game-theory strategy-stealing argument, being able to imitate a first player does not prove chess is a win for White: zugzwang means an extra move can be harmful.

facts.title: The alphabet stopped at h for a reason
facts.detail: Algebraic notation is a coordinate system, while older descriptive notation names squares from each player’s perspective. The same square could therefore have different descriptive names.

facts.title: A knight move has survived centuries
facts.detail: While the queen and bishop changed dramatically as modern chess evolved, the knight’s familiar leap is inherited from much earlier forms of the game.

facts.title: Opposite bishops can favor the attacker
facts.detail: Opposite-colored bishop endgames often draw, but in a middlegame the attacking bishop can operate on squares its rival can never defend. Queens and exposed kings change the story.

facts.title: A famous queen offer was declined
facts.detail: After Marshall’s 23...Qg3 in the 1912 Levitsky game, White resigned rather than capture the queen. The famous position is a threat calculation, not a queen blunder.

facts.title: A king marched into the middlegame
facts.detail: Against Timman in 1991, Nigel Short walked his king from g1 through h2, g3, f4 and g5. Its destination helped finish an attack while queens remained on the board.

facts.title: More than a lifetime of games
facts.detail: Shannon’s famous rough game-tree estimate is about 10¹²⁰. It is an estimate, not an exact count.

facts.title: Sometimes a queen is too much
facts.detail: Underpromotion can avoid stalemate or deliver a knight fork.

facts.title: A theoretical royal crowd
facts.detail: One side can theoretically have nine queens: the original plus eight promoted pawns.

facts.title: A one-move window
facts.detail: En passant is available only immediately after the opponent’s qualifying two-square pawn advance.

facts.title: An attacked rook can still castle
facts.detail: A rook being attacked does not by itself prevent castling.

facts.title: Three appearances, one claim
facts.detail: Threefold repetition can be claimed; the repeated positions need not be consecutive.

facts.title: Five means automatic
facts.detail: Fivefold repetition ends a standard game automatically under FIDE rules.

facts.title: A claim, not always an ending
facts.detail: The 50-move rule can be claimed after 50 moves by each side without a pawn move or capture.

facts.title: The automatic move limit
facts.detail: After 75 such moves by each side, the game is drawn; checkmate on the last move takes priority.

facts.title: Same pieces is not enough
facts.detail: Repetition also depends on whose turn it is and the available castling and en-passant rights.

facts.title: The board decides first
facts.detail: A legal move delivering checkmate ends the game immediately.

facts.title: A different first position
facts.detail: Chess960 has 960 starts; bishops begin on opposite colors, with the king between the rooks.

facts.title: Mate possible, force impossible
facts.detail: Two knights cannot force checkmate against a bare king with best defense.

facts.title: The right corner matters
facts.detail: Bishop-and-knight mate drives the king toward a corner matching the bishop’s color.

facts.title: One pawn can change everything
facts.detail: A rook pawn and the wrong-colored bishop can fail to beat a lone king.

facts.title: Kings fight without touching
facts.detail: Endgame opposition can force the other king to yield ground.

facts.title: The trouble with having a turn
facts.detail: In zugzwang, being required to move makes your position worse.

facts.title: An ancient ancestor
facts.detail: Chess traces its roots to chaturanga in India, around the sixth century.

facts.title: A game crossing borders
facts.detail: Shatranj carried an early form of chess through Persia and the Islamic world.

facts.title: The queen gained her power
facts.detail: The modern queen’s long-range movement emerged in Europe in the late fifteenth century.

facts.title: A very old chess book
facts.detail: Lucena’s 1497 book is an early printed source for modern chess rules and positions.

facts.title: The familiar silhouette
facts.detail: The Staunton piece design was introduced in 1849 and named after Howard Staunton.

facts.title: A new tournament era
facts.detail: Adolf Anderssen won London 1851, a landmark international chess tournament.

facts.title: A champion before the official title
facts.detail: Paul Morphy dominated his 1858 European tour before an official world championship existed.

facts.title: The first official world champion
facts.detail: Steinitz defeated Zukertort in the 1886 title match.

facts.title: Twenty-seven years at the top
facts.detail: Emanuel Lasker held the world title from 1894 to 1921.

facts.title: The chess machine
facts.detail: Capablanca became world champion in 1921, celebrated for clarity and endgame skill.

facts.title: A women’s championship pioneer
facts.detail: Vera Menchik won the first Women’s World Championship in 1927.

facts.title: A federation born in Paris
facts.detail: FIDE was founded in Paris in 1924.

facts.title: The first official grandmasters
facts.detail: FIDE awarded its first 27 grandmaster titles in 1950.

facts.title: A grandmaster milestone
facts.detail: Nona Gaprindashvili became the first woman awarded the open GM title in 1978.

facts.title: Breaking into the top ten
facts.detail: Judit Polgár reached the world top ten in the open rating list.

facts.title: A match on the world stage
facts.detail: Fischer and Spassky’s 1972 title match took place in Reykjavík, Iceland.

facts.title: Forty-eight games, no winner
facts.detail: The 1984–85 Karpov–Kasparov title match was stopped after 48 games without a champion being decided.

facts.title: A very long draw
facts.detail: Nikolić–Arsović, Belgrade 1989, lasted 269 moves.

facts.title: A computer wins a match
facts.detail: In 1997, Deep Blue defeated reigning champion Kasparov in a six-game classical match.

facts.title: Searching is not seeing everything
facts.detail: Chess engines search selected continuations; extra time can change the best move.

facts.title: Perfect knowledge, limited pieces
facts.detail: An endgame tablebase can give exact results for positions within its piece limit.

facts.title: A rating is relative
facts.detail: Elo measures results within a player pool; different pools are not automatically equivalent.

facts.title: Ratings arrived much later
facts.detail: Published FIDE Elo lists began long after the first world championship. Early champions have no title-era FIDE rating.

facts.title: One title again
facts.detail: Kramnik’s 2006 victory over Topalov reunited the split world championship.

facts.title: A teenage undisputed champion
facts.detail: Gukesh won the undisputed world title in 2024 at age 18.

milestones.title: An Indian beginning
milestones.detail: By about the sixth century, a game called chaturanga was played in India. Its Sanskrit name refers to four divisions of an army: infantry, cavalry, elephants, and chariots. Those pieces are ancestors of today’s pawns, knights, bishops, and rooks. The exact rules and date of origin remain uncertain.

milestones.title: A game travels
milestones.detail: Chess traveled from India to Persia and then through the Islamic world, where it was played as shatranj. Skilled players composed problems and recorded openings. In shatranj, the piece that became the queen moved only one square diagonally, making it far weaker than the modern queen.

milestones.title: The powerful queen era
milestones.detail: Luis Ramírez de Lucena’s book, printed in Salamanca around 1497, describes positions from both the older game and the emerging modern one. The queen and bishop had gained their long-range moves in Europe by this period. Players could now create threats much earlier, and opening mistakes became more costly.
milestones.imageArticle: Repetición de Amores y Arte de Ajedrez

milestones.title: The Mechanical Turk
milestones.detail: Wolfgang von Kempelen built the Turk for Empress Maria Theresa and first demonstrated it in 1770. It appeared to play chess by machinery, but a skilled player concealed inside controlled the moves. The device toured Europe and America and was destroyed by fire in Philadelphia in 1854.

milestones.title: The Staunton shape
milestones.detail: In 1849, London maker Jaques introduced a set based on Nathaniel Cooke’s design and endorsed by Howard Staunton. Its distinctive silhouettes made the pieces easier to identify across the board. The design became the model for the pieces used in most modern tournaments.

milestones.title: London gathers the masters
milestones.detail: Howard Staunton organized the 1851 London tournament during the year of the Great Exhibition. Sixteen players competed in a knockout format, and Adolf Anderssen defeated Marmaduke Wyvill in the final. The event showed that leading players from different countries could meet in a single organized international competition.

milestones.title: Morphy’s European tour
milestones.detail: After winning the First American Chess Congress, Paul Morphy traveled to Europe in 1858. He defeated leading players including Adolf Anderssen and Daniel Harrwitz. His Paris Opera Game illustrates a recurring strength of his play: rapid development and open lines mattered more than holding on to material.

milestones.title: The world title begins
milestones.detail: Wilhelm Steinitz and Johannes Zukertort played in New York, St. Louis, and New Orleans. The first player to win ten games would take the title. Steinitz recovered from a 4–1 deficit and won 10 games to 5, with five draws.

milestones.title: FIDE is founded
milestones.detail: FIDE was founded in Paris on July 20, 1924, during an international team chess tournament held alongside the Olympic Games. The new federation gave national associations a way to coordinate international competition. It later took responsibility for major titles, ratings, and international chess rules.

milestones.title: A women’s world title
milestones.detail: Vera Menchik won the inaugural Women’s World Chess Championship at the 1927 London Chess Olympiad. She retained the title until her death in 1944 and also competed in major open tournaments, where she defeated several leading players of her era.

milestones.title: A title decided by tournament
milestones.detail: Alexander Alekhine died in 1946 while still world champion. FIDE organized a five-player tournament in The Hague and Moscow to fill the vacancy. Mikhail Botvinnik won with 14 points from 20 games, beginning a period in which Soviet players dominated the title.

milestones.title: Official GM titles
milestones.detail: FIDE formally awarded the grandmaster title to 27 players in 1950. The first group included active stars and older players recognized for their past achievements. Later, the federation established a system with rating thresholds and tournament norms for earning the title.

milestones.title: Published Elo lists
milestones.detail: FIDE adopted the Elo system in 1970 and published its first official rating list in 1971. Named for physicist and chess player Arpad Elo, the system estimated a player’s expected score from the difference in ratings. Results against stronger and weaker opponents could now be compared on a common scale.

milestones.title: Reykjavík captures attention
milestones.detail: Bobby Fischer challenged Boris Spassky in Reykjavík at the height of the Cold War. After losing the first game and forfeiting the second, Fischer recovered to win the match 12½–8½. He became the first American-born official world champion.

milestones.title: A milestone for women
milestones.detail: Nona Gaprindashvili became the first woman awarded FIDE’s open grandmaster title in 1978. She had held the Women’s World Championship since 1962 and achieved strong results in open competition. In 1977 she shared first place at the Lone Pine International in California.

milestones.title: Kasparov takes the crown
milestones.detail: Garry Kasparov defeated Anatoly Karpov 13–11 in their 1985 rematch, becoming world champion at age 22. Their previous match had been stopped after 48 games without a winner. They met in three more title matches, and Kasparov held the classical title until 2000.

milestones.title: Two championship branches
milestones.detail: Garry Kasparov and challenger Nigel Short organized their 1993 match outside FIDE. FIDE staged its own championship, won by Anatoly Karpov against Jan Timman, while Kasparov defeated Short. The two title lines coexisted until 2006.

milestones.title: Deep Blue’s breakthrough
milestones.detail: IBM’s Deep Blue defeated reigning world champion Garry Kasparov 3½–2½ in their six-game 1997 rematch in New York. Kasparov had won their 1996 match. Deep Blue combined purpose-built hardware with rapid search and chess evaluation, and clinched the rematch by winning game six.

milestones.title: Reunification
milestones.detail: Classical champion Vladimir Kramnik and FIDE champion Veselin Topalov met in Elista to reunify the title. Their classical games ended 6–6. Kramnik won the rapid tiebreak 2½–1½, ending 13 years of rival championship lines.

milestones.title: The Carlsen era
milestones.detail: Magnus Carlsen defeated defending champion Viswanathan Anand 6½–3½ in Chennai. He won games five, six, and nine and drew the tenth to clinch the title. It was the first of Carlsen’s five world championship match victories.

milestones.title: Ding wins the tiebreak
milestones.detail: After Magnus Carlsen declined to defend his title, Ding Liren and Ian Nepomniachtchi contested the championship in Astana. They tied 7–7 in the classical games. Ding won the fourth rapid game with Black to take the tiebreak 2½–1½ and become China’s first open world champion.

milestones.title: A teenage champion
milestones.detail: Gukesh Dommaraju defeated defending champion Ding Liren 7½–6½ in Singapore. The match was level before the final scheduled game, when Gukesh converted a pawn ending after a late error by Ding. At 18, Gukesh became the youngest undisputed world champion.

champions.highlight: Awarded the title; defends it in 1978
